beats.headline: Stop polling your database every two seconds!
beats.subline: Short polling burns CPU and kills your latency. Here is how to push data efficiently.
beats.narration: If fifty thousand users poll your API for updates, you are burning CPU on TLS and auth for empty responses. Stop the polling. Use WebSockets or SSE to push data only when it changes.

beats.title: SSE vs. WebSockets

bottom.label: WebSockets
bottom.code:
GET /ws HTTP/1.1
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade

beats.narration: SSE is simple, unidirectional, and runs over standard HTTP. Use it for dashboards or notifications. WebSockets provide a full-duplex pipe for interactive apps like chat or multiplayer games.

beats.title: The 101 Handshake
beats.subtitle: Upgrading HTTP to a persistent socket
beats.narration: WebSockets start as an HTTP GET request. The server validates the handshake key and returns a 101 Switching Protocols status. From that point, the connection is no longer HTTP—it is a binary frame stream.

beats.title: Spring SseEmitter

steps.explanation: Releases the Servlet thread back to the pool immediately.
Flushes UTF-8 text chunks directly to the client.

beats.narration: SseEmitter is your best friend for server-to-client streams. It releases the request thread, keeping your memory footprint low while maintaining thousands of open connections.

beats.headline: Why your WebSocket app breaks in production.
beats.subline: In-memory brokers fail as soon as you add a second pod. Here is the fix.
beats.narration: If you use an in-memory broker, your app will fail in Kubernetes. Alice connects to Pod A, Bob to Pod B, and they never see each other's messages. Let's fix that.

beats.title: The Scaling Problem
beats.subtitle: Why SimpleBroker is not enough
beats.narration: SimpleBroker keeps subscriptions in local JVM memory. In a cluster, pods can't talk. You need a STOMP broker relay like RabbitMQ to act as the shared message bus for all pods.

beats.title: StompBrokerRelay Config

steps.explanation: Swaps local memory for a persistent TCP connection to RabbitMQ.
Points to the STOMP plugin port on your broker cluster.

beats.narration: Enable the STOMP plugin in RabbitMQ and configure your Spring app to relay frames. Now, when Alice sends a message, it hits the broker and fans out to every pod in your cluster.

beats.title: RabbitMQ Setup
beats.caption: Enable the STOMP plugin
beats.narration: Don't forget to enable the STOMP plugin. It listens on port 61613 by default. Without this, your Spring relay will have nowhere to send its frames.

takeaways: Relay to RabbitMQ for horizontal scale

beats.headline: Never put JWTs in your WebSocket URL.
beats.subline: They end up in logs, browser history, and APM traces. Here is the secure way.
beats.narration: Putting tokens in the URL is a security nightmare. They end up in Nginx logs and browser history. Use a ChannelInterceptor to validate tokens in the STOMP CONNECT frame instead.

beats.title: Channel Interceptor Auth

steps.explanation: Extracts STOMP headers from the incoming frame.
Reads the Bearer token from the secure STOMP header.

beats.narration: The ChannelInterceptor intercepts the CONNECT frame. You extract the Authorization header, validate the JWT, and set the user principal. This keeps your tokens out of the URL.

beats.title: Auth Patterns
beats.narration: Always prefer headers over query params. Headers are encrypted inside the WebSocket tunnel, keeping your sensitive identity data away from prying eyes in your infrastructure logs.

beats.title: The Auth Flow
beats.subtitle: Securing the handshake
beats.narration: The interceptor acts as a gatekeeper. If the JWT is invalid, the connection is rejected before any subscription or message frames are processed. This is your first line of defense.

beats.headline: Why your SSE events arrive in a burst.
beats.subline: Nginx buffering is likely the culprit. Here is how to disable it.
beats.narration: If your SSE events seem frozen and then arrive all at once, Nginx is buffering your response. You must disable this to get real-time delivery.

beats.title: Nginx SSE Config
beats.caption: Disable buffering for real-time
beats.narration: Nginx buffers by default. Set proxy buffering off and disable gzip for your SSE location. This forces Nginx to flush every event chunk to the client immediately.

beats.title: Preventing Memory Leaks

steps.explanation: Crucial: remove dead emitters to prevent heap exhaustion.

beats.narration: If you don't remove dead emitters, your memory will grow until the JVM crashes. Always attach cleanup callbacks to handle completion, timeout, and errors.

beats.title: OSIV Danger
beats.narration: Disable Open-Session-in-View. If enabled, your DB connection stays open for the entire lifetime of the SSE stream, which could be hours. That will starve your connection pool instantly.
